summary: Defines MIB objects for managing GSMP. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3295 describes the SNMP objects that manage the General Switch Management Protocol, which controls a label switch. It tells a manager which tables to fill in to start a session, what to read to follow a session, and which notifications arrive when something changes.

subtitle: The SNMP objects that let a manager configure and watch label switch sessions.

tldr.problem: The General Switch Management Protocol lets a controller set up and tear down label switched connections, but a network manager needs a way to configure and monitor those sessions with SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIB module with tables for switch controller entities, switch entities, their encapsulations and the sessions between them, together with counters and notifications for session and port events.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3295 is a Proposed Standard from June 2002 and has been updated by RFC 9141.

today: RFC 3295 is a Proposed Standard from June 2002 and has been updated by RFC 9141. It defines the managed objects for GSMP version 3, the version of the protocol specified in RFC 3292.

sections.title: What the MIB Covers
sections.content:
The RFC defines a portion of the Management Information Base, the virtual store of named values that network management protocols read and write, for use with the Internet network management protocols. In particular, it describes managed objects for the General Switch Management Protocol, defined in RFC 3292.

The objects it defines are the management side of GSMP. A manager uses them to set up a controller, a switch and the connection between them, to follow what happens on that connection, and to be told when something important changes.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is a set of named values that a management program can read and change on a device. This RFC says which named values describe a GSMP session, and how a manager uses them.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework
sections.content:
The SNMP management framework has five major parts. There is an overall architecture, described in RFC 2571. There are mechanisms for describing and naming objects and events, the Structure of Management Information, whose first version is SMIv1 and whose second version is SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580. There are message protocols for transferring management information, SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3. There are protocol operations for accessing management information, and a set of fundamental applications described in RFC 2573, along with the view-based access control mechanism described in RFC 2575.

Managed objects are reached through the MIB, and objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms of the SMI. This RFC specifies a MIB module that complies with SMIv2. A MIB complying with SMIv1 can be produced through the appropriate translations, and the translated MIB must be semantically equivalent, except where objects or events are dropped because no translation is possible, such as the use of Counter64. Some machine-readable information in SMIv2 becomes text in SMIv1 during translation, and that loss is not considered to change the semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is built from an architecture, a way of describing objects, message formats, operations on those objects, and a set of standard applications. This MIB is written in the second version of the object description language, and can be translated to the first for older equipment.

sections.title: GSMP Sessions and Entities
sections.content:
GSMP is a general purpose protocol for controlling a label switch. It lets a controller establish and release connections across the switch, manage switch ports, and request configuration information or statistics. It also lets the switch tell the controller about asynchronous events such as a link going down.

The protocol is asymmetric: the controller is the master and the switch is the slave. Several switches may be controlled by one controller, using several instantiations of the protocol over separate control connections. A switch may also be controlled by more than one controller, using the technique of partitioning.

Each instance of a switch controller and switch partition adjacency is a session between one switch controller entity and one switch entity. The MIB provides objects to configure and set up these entities so that the sessions form, and objects to monitor the sessions once they exist.
sections.plainLanguage: GSMP lets a controller set up and release connections across a label switch and hear about events such as a link failure. The controller drives and the switch follows. Every pairing of a controller with a switch is a session, and the MIB has objects to create them and to watch them.

sections.title: What the MIB Leaves Out
sections.content:
The GSMP MIB is a protocol MIB. It holds objects to configure, monitor and maintain the GSMP protocol entity. It does not provide information learned through the protocol, such as the configuration of all ports.

The relationships between virtual entities, such as virtual switch entities, and physical ones, such as switch entities, fall outside the management of GSMP, and the same applies to the management of switch partitions.

It is possible to configure which switch controllers control a switch, and how many, because every potential session with the switch has to be represented by a switch entity. It is not possible to define that one switch controller must not allow another controller to control the same switch or partition. The RFC assumes that mechanisms exist to synchronise controllers and their configuration, and leaves that outside the scope of the MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB manages the protocol itself, not the traffic that flows through the switch. It also does not stop two controllers from both claiming the same switch; keeping controllers in step is somebody else's job.

sections.title: Configuring a Session with SNMP
sections.content:
Two tables configure potential GSMP sessions, one for a manager acting as a switch controller and one for a manager acting as a switch. Each row in them starts a GSMP session.

The entity ID is a 48-bit name that is unique within the operational context of the device. A 48-bit IEEE 802 MAC address may be used if one is available, and if Ethernet encapsulation is used the entity ID must be the MAC address of the interface on which the session is to be set up.

The encapsulation of the potential session is defined first. For ATM, a row in gsmpAtmEncapTable is created with the index set to the entity ID, and the specified resources are allocated to GSMP. For TCP/IP, a row in gsmpTcpIpEncapTable is created with the index set to the entity ID, and the specified port is allocated to GSMP. No special action is needed for Ethernet encapsulation.

The entity information comes next. An entry in gsmpSwitchTable creates a switch entity, and an entry in gsmpControllerTable creates a switch controller entity, both with the index set to the entity ID. When the row status of one of those entries is set to active, the adjacency protocol of GSMP starts.

A further table, gsmpSessionTable, shows the sessions that are established or being established. Each row represents one session between an entity and a peer, and carries the peer information, the session state, parameters negotiated by the adjacency procedures and statistics for the session.

All GSMP managers should create rows in this order, because it avoids clashes when several SNMP managers create competing entries in the same tables. Entities configured by other means, such as a command line, should still be represented as rows in these tables and should be possible to query, and may be possible to change with SNMP.
sections.plainLanguage: To start a session, a manager first reserves the transport, then creates the controller or switch row, and only then activates the row, which starts the handshake. The order matters, because two managers working at once can otherwise create conflicting entries.

sections.title: The MIB Groups
sections.content:
The MIB is divided into five groups.

The Switch Controller group configures a potential session on a controller. A row in gsmpControllerTable is created for each session, and with ATM or TCP/IP encapsulation a matching row must exist in the encapsulation tables before the adjacency protocol starts. The adjacency parameters include the maximum supported GSMP version, the time between periodic adjacency messages, the controller's local port number and instance number, whether partitions are used and which partition, and the resynchronisation strategy for the session. A notification mapping is set to say which events produce which SNMP notifications.

The Switch group configures a potential session on the switch, in the same way, with a row in gsmpSwitchTable. Its parameters add the switch name and the switch type, and a suggested maximum window size for unacknowledged request messages.

The Encapsulation groups hold the transport-specific data: the ATM table specifies the interface and virtual channel, and the TCP/IP table specifies the IP address and port number. The MIB may be extended with new encapsulations, standard or proprietary, and a new one should be added as a new table indexed by the entity ID, whose row is created before any entity row that uses it.

The General group holds the session table, which monitors and maintains GSMP sessions, each defined by a pair of a switch controller entity and a switch entity.

The Notifications group defines the notifications that let a device tell the management station about status changes, one for each type of GSMP event.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is split into five groups: one for the controller side, one for the switch side, one for the transport details, one for the session table, and one for the notifications.

sections.title: Definitions and Textual Conventions
sections.content:
The module is called GSMP-MIB and sits at mib-2 98. It has four branches: gsmpNotifications, gsmpObjects, gsmpNotificationsObjects and gsmpConformance.

Five textual conventions are defined for the convenience of people reading the MIB. GsmpNameType is the 48-bit name used for entities. GsmpPartitionType says whether partitions are used and how the partition ID is negotiated, with the values noPartition, fixedPartitionRequest and fixedPartitionAssigned. GsmpPartitionIdType is the 8-bit partition ID, whose format GSMP does not define; the RFC notes that it could be split into sub-identifiers, so that a 6-bit partition number and a 2-bit sub-identifier would give a switch 64 partitions with 4 available IDs each. GsmpVersion names the protocol versions, 1 for GSMPv1.1, 2 for GSMPv2.0 and 3 for GSMPv3, with other numbers possible later. GsmpLabelType holds a label, which is a type-length-value tuple of a 2-octet type field, a 2-octet length field and a variable-length value, and a label field may be a stack of such labels.

Objects that use these conventions are still encoded by the rules of their primitive type, so the conventions carry no special meaning to SNMP and do not require any change to the SMI or to SNMP.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB defines a few reusable data types so that the objects below read clearly: a 48-bit name, a partition type and ID, a protocol version and a label. They are only shorthand for readers and change nothing about how SNMP works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Assuming secure network management such as SNMPv3 is in place, the objects in this MIB do not threaten the security of the network.

Many of the objects have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, so they may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments, and support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

Several managed objects may hold sensitive information, in the gsmpControllerTable and the gsmpSwitchTable. It is therefore important to control even read access to these objects, and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network with SNMP. Not all versions of SNMP provide the features needed for that. SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment, and even when the network itself is secure, for example with IPsec, there is no control over who on that network may read or change the objects in this MIB.

The RFC recommends the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, specifically the User-based Security Model of RFC 2574 and the View-based Access Control Model of RFC 2575. It then leaves it to the operator to make sure that the SNMP entity giving access to this MIB is configured so that only principals with legitimate rights can read or change its objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB holds nothing secret by itself, but a manager can change how the switch behaves, and some entries reveal configuration. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with its access control, and leaves the setting of who may read or change what to the operator.

viz.caption: THE BRANCHES OF THE GSMP MIB MODULE
THE FIVE GROUPS OF THE MIB

items.title: Switch Controller
items.text: One row per potential session on the controller, with its adjacency parameters.

items.title: Switch
items.text: One row per potential session on the switch, with its adjacency parameters.

items.title: Encapsulation
items.text: The ATM and TCP/IP tables holding the transport details of each session.

items.title: General
items.text: The session table, which monitors and maintains running sessions.

items.title: Notifications
items.text: One notification for each type of GSMP event.

viz.caption: THE NOTIFICATIONS DEFINED BY THE MIB

items.label: Session established
items.desc: Sent when a new session is established.

items.label: Session ended
items.desc: Sent when a session terminates, with the final accounting statistics.

items.label: Send failure
items.desc: Sent when a message with a failure indication was sent.

items.label: Receive failure
items.desc: Sent when a message with a failure indication was received.

items.label: Port up
items.desc: Sent when a port up event is received or sent.

items.label: Port down
items.desc: Sent when a port down event is received or sent.

items.label: Invalid label
items.desc: Sent when an invalid label event is received or sent.

items.label: New port
items.desc: Sent when a new port event is received or sent.

items.label: Dead port
items.desc: Sent when a dead port event is received or sent.

items.label: Adjacency update
items.desc: Sent when an adjacency update event is received or sent.
